title: Rail-to-Rail Op-Amps, Phase Reversal, Slew Rate, and the LM358 vs LM393 Pinout Trap
subtitle: How to avoid clipping, input crossover distortion, slew-induced full-power bandwidth collapse, and catastrophic op-amp/comparator confusion on SOIC-8 and SOT-23-5 boards.
summary: Dual SOIC-8 operational amplifiers and comparators share one of the most standardized pinouts in electronics — which makes substituting them dangerously deceptive. This engineering guide breaks down rail-to-rail input/output headroom limits, JFET phase reversal, GBWP versus slew-rate full-power bandwidth, zero-drift chopper quirks, and why LM358DR and LM393DR are NEVER drop-in replacements despite identical pin assignments.
key_takeaways: LM358DR (dual push-pull op-amp) and LM393DR (dual open-collector comparator) have the EXACT same 8-pin SOIC-8 pinout, yet swapping them breaks circuits: LM393DR cannot pull high without an external pull-up resistor and oscillates violently in linear negative-feedback loops because it lacks internal frequency compensation.

Never replace a 32 V–36 V op-amp (LM358DR, TL072IDR, OPA2134UA) with a 5.5 V low-voltage CMOS RRIO part (LMV358IDR, TLV9002IDR) without verifying supply rails — 12 V or +/-15 V rails destroy 5.5 V CMOS silicon instantly.
Small-signal bandwidth f_-3dB = GBWP / A_CL does NOT guarantee large-signal fidelity: large sinusoidal swings distort into triangles above the Full-Power Bandwidth f_FPBW = SR / (2 * pi * V_peak).

Rail-to-rail output (RRO) never reaches literally 0.000 V or V+ under resistive load (saturation scales as I_load * R_ds,on), and dual-stage rail-to-rail input (RRI) amplifiers exhibit a Vos crossover step roughly 0.7–1.2 V below V+.

sections.heading: 1. The Classic SOIC-8 Trap: LM358DR vs LM393DR (Identical Pinout, Incompatible Silicon)
body: Nearly every dual op-amp and dual comparator in an 8-pin SOIC-8 package obeys the industry-standard pinout: Pin 1 = OUT_A, Pin 2 = IN-_A, Pin 3 = IN+_A, Pin 4 = V-/GND, Pin 5 = IN+_B, Pin 6 = IN-_B, Pin 7 = OUT_B, Pin 8 = V+/VCC. That uniformity leads junior engineers — and naive distributor cross-reference tables — straight into the infamous LM358DR versus LM393DR mistake.

Although LM358DR and LM393DR share identical SOIC-8 pin numbers and nearly identical 3 V to 32 V (or 36 V) supply ranges, their internal architectures serve opposite jobs. LM358DR is a frequency-compensated linear operational amplifier with a push-pull (totem-pole) output stage capable of both sourcing and sinking current smoothly inside negative-feedback loops. LM393DR is a dedicated voltage comparator with NO internal Miller compensation capacitor and an OPEN-COLLECTOR NPN output transistor that can only sink current to GND.

Drop an LM393DR into an LM358DR unity-gain buffer or non-inverting amplifier PCB and two failures occur immediately: first, the output cannot drive high at all without an external pull-up resistor to VCC; second, even if you add a pull-up resistor, the uncompensated open-loop phase shift exceeds 180 degrees well before unity gain, turning your amplifier into a megahertz relaxation oscillator. Conversely, substituting an LM358DR into an LM393DR comparator circuit causes sluggish 10–50 us overdrive recovery, fails wired-OR / level-shifting open-collector logic (driving 12 V straight into a 3.3 V MCU GPIO pin!), and risks internal input clamp damage on differential overdrive.

callout.title: Pin-Compatible Does NOT Mean Electrically Substitutable
callout.text: Pin2Pin Global strictly blocks Level 1 Candidate Drop-In status whenever device_kind (opamp vs comparator) or output_type (push-pull vs open-collector) differs. LM358DR vs LM393DR and LMV358IDR vs LM393DR always trigger a CRITICAL output-stage & stability warning.

sections.heading: 2. Rail-to-Rail Reality: Input Common-Mode Crossover & Output Headroom
body: Legacy 32 V bipolar op-amps like LM358DR handle inputs down to GND (0 V), but their upper input common-mode range stops roughly 1.5 V to 2.0 V below V+, and their output stage saturates roughly 1.5 V below V+ under load. On a 3.3 V single-supply microcontroller ADC front end, an LM358DR can only swing from ~0.05 V up to ~1.8 V — throwing away nearly half of your 12-bit ADC dynamic range! Worse, the LM358 Class-B output stage exhibits severe zero-crossing crossover distortion unless externally biased with a pull-down resistor.

Upgrading a 3.3 V or 5 V rail from LM358DR to a modern CMOS Rail-to-Rail Input/Output (RRIO) op-amp like TLV9002IDR (1.8–5.5 V, RRIO, 60 uA/ch) or LMV358IDR (2.7–5.5 V, RRO) recovers nearly the full 0–3.3 V ADC span — provided your supply rail never exceeds 5.5 V. If your board runs from 9 V or 12 V and still requires RRIO swing, neither LMV358IDR nor TLV9002IDR survives; instead, select a wider-supply bipolar RRIO part like MC33202DR2G (1.8–12 V) which delivers rail-to-rail input and output headroom without 5.5 V breakdown.

Keep two subtle rail-to-rail physics caveats in mind. First, 'Rail-to-Rail Output' still obeys Ohm's law across the output MOSFETs' R_ds,on: driving a heavy 2 kOhm load at 3.3 V (1.65 mA) drops 50–150 mV inside the output stage, so never expect literally 0.000 V or 3.300 V under load. Second, 'Rail-to-Rail Input' CMOS op-amps use two parallel input differential pairs (a PMOS pair active near GND and an NMOS pair active near V+). As your common-mode input sweeps across the handover threshold (~0.8 V to 1.2 V below V+), input offset voltage Vos jumps abruptly by several hundred microvolts, degrading CMRR and introducing THD in non-inverting unity-gain buffers. Inverting amplifier topologies eliminate this crossover error completely because the inputs stay fixed at a constant mid-rail virtual ground.

sections.heading: 3. JFET Phase Reversal: Why TL072IDR vs OPA2134UA Matters in Control Loops
body: Phase reversal is one of the nastiest analog failure modes in industrial control and audio circuits. When the input voltage of a classic JFET-input op-amp (historically epitomized by legacy TL072 designs) drops below its negative common-mode limit — typically within ~3 V of the negative supply V- — the input JFET gate-channel junction forward-biases, inverting the polarity of the differential stage. The output abruptly slams all the way to the POSITIVE rail (+15 V) instead of clamping quietly at the negative rail (-15 V).

In a servo motor loop, PID heater controller, or audio limiter, phase reversal turns negative feedback into positive latch-up, pinning the actuator at 100% hard over until power is cycled. Modern upgraded silicon like OPA2134UA (TI's SoundPlus FET-input audio op-amp, 8 MHz GBWP, 20 V/us slew rate, 0.00008% THD+N) and newer revised TL072H/CMOS families incorporate internal phase-reversal protection clamps. Whenever you migrate an older split-rail (+/-12 V or +/-15 V) board from TL072IDR to OPA2134UA, verify quiescent current increase (~4 mA/ch vs ~1.4 mA/ch) and power dissipation — while enjoying clean, phase-reversal-free headroom and dramatically lower noise.

sections.heading: 4. Small-Signal GBWP vs Large-Signal Slew Rate (Full-Power Bandwidth)
body: Engineers frequently pick an op-amp by checking only Gain-Bandwidth Product (GBWP) and verifying f_-3dB = GBWP / A_CL >= 10 * f_signal. That guarantees small-signal gain flatness (say for a 50 mVpp sine wave), yet completely ignores large-signal Slew Rate (SR) limiting!

For a sine wave V(t) = V_peak * sin(2 * pi * f * t), the steepest slope occurs at zero crossing: dV/dt_max = 2 * pi * f * V_peak. If that required slope exceeds the op-amp's Slew Rate (in V/us), the output cannot keep up and collapses into a distorted triangle wave with severe harmonic distortion and phase lag. Rearranging yields the Full-Power Bandwidth: f_FPBW = SR / (2 * pi * V_peak).

Plug in real pilot numbers for a 20 kHz, 10 V_peak audio line driver (V_peak = 10 V): required slew rate is 2 * pi * 20,000 * 10 = 1.26 V/us. A classic LM358DR (SR ~0.3–0.5 V/us) hits its full-power ceiling at just f_FPBW = 0.5e6 / (2 * pi * 10) = 7.96 kHz — severely slewing every cymbal crash above 8 kHz! Upgrading to OPA2134UA (SR = 20 V/us) raises full-power bandwidth to 318 kHz, providing >15x slew headroom. Similarly, on a 3.3 V single-supply 500 kHz active filter with V_peak = 1.5 V, required slew rate is 2 * pi * 500,000 * 1.5 = 4.71 V/us: TLV9001IDBVR (1 MHz, 2 V/us) clips and distorts, whereas dropping in its pin-compatible higher-speed sibling TLV9061IDBVR (10 MHz, 6.5 V/us, SOT-23-5 DBV) cleanly clears both GBWP and slew budgets.

callout.title: Watch Bandwidth & Zero-Drift Chopper Tradeoffs When Swapping SOT-23-5 Single Op-Amps
callout.text: TLV9001IDBVR (1 MHz), TLV9061IDBVR (10 MHz), and OPA333AIDBVR (350 kHz zero-drift chopper) all share the standard TI DBV SOT-23-5 pinout (1=OUT, 2=V-, 3=IN+, 4=IN-, 5=V+), yet behave completely differently! OPA333AIDBVR gives ultra-low 10 uV max offset for microvolt strain-gauge/shunt bridges, but its ~125 kHz internal chopping clock injects tiny current glitches into >100 kOhm source impedances and its 0.16 V/us slew rate cannot handle fast AC signals. Conversely, jumping from 1 MHz TLV9001 to 10 MHz TLV9061 into a heavy capacitive cable load (>100 pF) can cause ringing unless you add a 22–100 Ohm series isolation resistor R_iso.

sections.heading: 5. Pre-Swap Analog Verification Checklist
body: Before finalizing any op-amp cross-reference on a schematic or prototype:
1. Verify Device Kind & Output Stage: Confirm push-pull op-amp vs open-collector/open-drain comparator; never mix LM358DR/LMV358IDR with LM393DR.
2. Check Supply Span & Absolute Max: Confirm total (V+ - V-) stays within recommended limits (especially separating 5.5 V CMOS parts from 12 V–36 V bipolar/JFET parts).

3. Check Both GBWP and Slew Rate: Run Pin2Pin Global's Op-Amp GBWP & Slew-Rate Checker with your exact closed-loop gain A_CL, maximum signal frequency f_sig, and peak output amplitude V_peak to guarantee both small-signal bandwidth and full-power slew margin.

4. Audit Input Bias Current (Ib) vs Source Impedance: Replacing a pA-class CMOS/JFET op-amp (TLV9002IDR, TL072IDR, OPA2134UA) with a 20 nA–100 nA BJT op-amp (LM358DR, MC33202DR2G) across a 1 MOhm pH probe or photodiode transimpedance resistor creates a 20 mV–100 mV DC error (V_err = Ib * R_source).

5. Test Capacitive Load Stability on the Bench: Apply a small 100 mVpp square wave at 10 kHz to the op-amp input and check output step overshoot (<15% overshoot ensures healthy >50 degrees phase margin).
